# Copper July 2010 

- While there has been considerably less volatility in copper markets this month compared to June, prices have generally trended upwards under mildly improving fundamentals or, at least, the impression of such.  Average LME cash quotes to July 26<sup>th</sup> edged up by $70/t on June to c.$6600/t, and the closing price of $7126/t on the 26<sup>th</sup> of this month was $300/t higher than June’s peak on the 28<sup>th</sup> .  At that level, we are close to matching this year’s _average_ cash price of $7253/t, and this marks a turnaround in the mildly bearish sentiment that has hung over the market since the middle of May.  Furthermore, the contango narrowed this month from an average of $30/t in June to $20/t. 

- There have been mixed interpretations of the economic data emerging from China for June.  Because recent data have generally shown month-on-month declines, it has been easy to take the view that the Chinese economy is running out of steam.  Our view is that this “downturn” has been well engineered by the Chinese authorities who are steering for a soft economic landing for the next few months, but copper demand will still rise by over 9% this year. 

- Events of the past month have created a far more positive outlook for the copper market moving forward (and certainly more optimistic than many macro indicators might suggest).  Demand remains surprisingly strong in most developed economies supported by ongoing inventory adjustments and a general lack of scrap.  Chinese consumption is clearly slowing but from unsustainably high levels and not at the sort of rates that were initially feared. 

- Market commentators have observed a “softening” in the concentrates market due to a general lack of buying interest.  In reality, the market continues to operate on a two-tier basis with China and India at the fore given their willingness to purchase material at terms that are well below what the rest of the industry are prepared, or indeed can afford to pay.  The “softening” therefore relates to the general reluctance to purchase material by these two dominant spot market players.  Spot rates in China have thus risen over the past month to approximately $20/t & 2c/lb

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper prices trend up in July…** While there has been considerably less volatility in copper markets this month compared to June, prices have generally trended upwards under mildly improving fundamentals or, at least, the impression of such.  Average LME cash quotes to July 26<sup>th</sup> edged up by $70/t on June to c.$6600/t, and the closing price of $7126/t on the 26<sup>th</sup> of this month was $300/t higher than June’s peak on the 28<sup>th</sup> .  At that level, we are close to matching this year’s _average_ cash price of $7253/t, and this marks a turnaround in the mildly bearish sentiment that has hung over the market since the middle of May.  Furthermore, the contango narrowed this month from an average of $30/t in June to $20/t. 

**..but it did not start out this way** However, the first week of the month did not show such promise.  Generally poor global economic data for May forced metals prices down in the final days of June and into the first week of July, with cash testing two-week lows right on the opening day of the month at $6354/t.  The news from the International Wrought Copper Council on the 5<sup>th</sup> that Western World copper demand will not recover until 2011-2012 could have sent the market into another low.  Instead, the market shrugged off that figure and took the IWCC’s global demand growth forecast for this year of 2.3% and a further 4.1% in 2011 as neutral, possibly even supportive, given the three-week spate of discouraging economic statistics.  Indeed, from mid-month, once all discussion of macro-economic difficulties such as Euroland debt and gloomy employment figures had run its course, we saw a sudden return of interest in the traditional fundamentals behind copper itself. 

**China comes back into the market** The concern that the Chinese government was forcing its over-heated economy to cool down too dramatically had generated a gathering impression that metals demand would suffer this year.  While there are several layers of statistics to show that China had retreated somewhat, it was not true to say that the country had ever gone away.  In managing a soft economic landing, China has reduced its appetite for imports of all metals in recent months; high grade copper cathode imports of 1.302Mt through to June, for example, were down by 10.1% during H1 2010 over the prior year, while standard grade cathode imports of 229kt were off by almost 25%.  But last year’s lower prices actively encouraged heavy buying and re-stocking, whereas H1 2010’s average prices have been higher, prompting China to go through a de-stocking phase.  Meanwhile, the comparatively low 16.9% _increase_ in scrap imports to 2.031Mt easily outweighs a 25.6% decline in imports of rods, bars and shapes (to 6.6kt).  Indeed, in our view, there have been some signs this month that China has been returning to the global primary and scrap markets since mid-June, an

d this has been a contributing factor to the price strengthening witnessed this month on the LME as well as premia in other markets. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

**SHFE, LME stocks fall again** In line with the trend of recent weeks, warehouse stocks have continued to fall and have been the most visible fundamental feature behind the stronger prices. Shanghai exchange stocks to the 22nd declined to a level last seen in early February (114kt) and were down by over 10kt on the month; a further 26.2kt remains on warrant. LME stock levels have seen a net reduction of almost 7.5% this month to 416kt since the last day of June, and this represents the lowest point of the year. As in June, warehouses in New Orleans saw the largest declines, from 180kt at the end of June to under 169kt. With a further 33.5kt of cancelled warrants (8% of stocks and the most of all LME metals, 16.7kt of which are in New Orleans), we would expect this trend to continue. Meanwhile, Comex-held stocks held steady at 92.5kt. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2010 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Equity markets support metals prices** With stocks falling and murmurs in the market of demand firming, other economic indicators once again kicked in by the middle of the month to be supportive of metals prices across the LME complex. A strong performance by US equities on the 20th , plus better data out of China, overcame poor news from Japan; on the 21st , a rally in the mining sector-driven UK FTSE pushed metals higher again and prompted technical short covering. Somewhat dispiriting comments by the US Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke on the 22nd took US equities and commodities lower, but trading in Asia breathed life into metals again, and copper began its current rally. **Arbitrage opportunities become fewer by month end** As we have noted since early May, SHFE/LME arbitrage conditions have been favourable and remained so for most of this month. From our sources, we understand that Chinese buying stepped up in the first half of the month as the arbitrage widened and as it became increasingly difficult to source cathode either from warehouses or by direct spot sales. Thus far in July LME quotes have averaged $79/t below SHFE prices (exclusive of VAT) through to the 27th . However, since the 22nd July LME cash quotes have traded an average $53/t above SHFE prices (exclusive of VAT). #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 Ref

**Chinese premia continue to strengthen** Consequently, cathode premia in China continued to rise from our noted $120-130/t in June to $140-150/t this month. Supporting this, though, have been more than the odd comment from our contacts that global cathode producers are keeping a keen eye on spot sales in order to protect both term contract prices and spot premia levels. It is hard to say whether there is much truth to this, but one consequence will be that if metal _users_ cannot get the primary material they need because of the effect of competitive pressure from arbitrage players tying up product, some of them will have to turn to the secondary market for feed. **Chinese might turn to US for low-grade scrap…** For the Chinese, this typically means heading to the US market for scrap copper. Even into the first week of this month, though, the scrap market was pretty quiet, with most buyers from China, India and South Korea showing limited interest. No. 2 birch/cliff material was reportedly selling domestically for Comex minus 32 c/lb, and if sales were ongoing to China, these would go for Comex less 22 c/lb. Although interest has picked up from Chinese buyers, the levels are still not that dramatic, and we will need to wait for Chinese trade figures for July to see if buyers have turned to secondaries this month to plug that expected gap in refined metal. **..but better-quality scrap remains tight in the US…** What _is_ of interest in the US scrap market this month, though, is the ongoing tightness in better quality scrap grades, as preferred by US tube mills. Bare bright quality material was selling in June at a discount to Comex of 5-8 c/lb, but current quotes are seeing that discount reduced to 1-2 c/lb, or even flat if prompt delivery is required. Explanations we have heard for this smaller discount, given that exports of such qualities remain low, include lower manufacturing rates and hence lower scrap generation, and a reluctance among scrap collectors and traders to release material in the hope of securing better prices once industrial activity rates pick up, following the ongoing seasonal shut-downs. **..pushing US metal premia even higher** With this stress in scrap markets, upward pressure on primary metal (cathode) premia has followed. This month they have risen from June’s 4.5-5.5 c/lb to 5.0-7.5 c/lb. But aside from the tightness in certain scrap grades, we have heard other reasons for this strength in premia. Last month’s excuse of tight freight conditions due to trucks getting better rates from competing agricultural markets has been pushed aside by a general comment that lower economic activity over the past 18 months has forced many truckers out of business – i.e. t

here are fewer trucks for everyone for prompt delivery. A second explanation mirrors one that we commented on above Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2010 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update regarding less metal being made available into the spot market by producers who want to support prices. One source we spoke with even went as far as saying that US producers were selling little more than contracted tonnages and rejecting spot sales in order to keep the market deliberately tight. #### **Copper Spot Premia ($/t)** 200 W Europe Shanghai US c/lb 10

**Other factors hold up US premia too** However, we believe that at least two other forces have come into play here that are keeping premia on a rising trend. First, as we have heard across other metals, end-users signed on for lower than normal contract tonnage during 2009 and into 2010 as they were concerned about holding stock during a time of demand uncertainty. However, business rates have performed better than expected, and yet the only way to satisfy orders is to turn to the spot market for primary metal, especially as scrap alternatives are pretty tight too. **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

oing forward.  Besides this, we have seen no copper anodes from Vale’s Sudbury (due to the now-resolved strike over the past 12 months) being delivered to Xstrata’s CCR refinery, and Xstrata has also re-directed additional anodes from its Altonorte smelter in Chile to Townsville, Australia away from CCR in Canada because of low intermediate feed from Mt Isa (see PRODUCTION).  This unique set of circumstances has added up to a considerable loss of copper cathode into the northern industrial heartland of the US.  Consequently, this has changed the geographic buying pattern, as now more buyers have had to source material from the Gulf area, and this no doubt goes some way to explaining the continued exit of cathode out of New Orleans warehouses (see page 2). 

**European premia strengthen** As in the USA, copper cathode premia in Europe are also strengthening and share similar reasons as to why.  Grade A cathode premia have moved up from $60-80/t seen at the end of last month to levels of $75-90/t now.  There does seem to be a slight north-south divide, though, with stronger northern re-stocking in the autos sector prompting good demand for winding wire, enamelled wire and conductor strip and a resurgence in demand from the power cable segment.  Many manufacturers of wire rod, cake and billet have reported stronger than expected order books, even if demand is clearly not back up to pre-crisis levels. 

**Tight scrap and stronger spot market in Europe also support premia** Again, as with the USA, we are hearing quite consistent reports in Europe of tighter than expected scrap markets, which brings primary metal back into users’ sights. Added to this pressure is the higher call on spot material given the lower amounts of cathode taken on contract during 2009 and into 2010.  A lot of contracted cathode output was booked ahead of plant shutdowns, leaving spot sellers able to obtain higher premia. 

**Chinese demand will lead the way as mature economies wait for real end-use demand growth…** In light of the stronger demand for primary copper seen during this second quarter, and the building potential for some resilience in the market due to the widespread tightness in scrap, it is quite possible that our forecast global demand growth for this year of 6.3% may end up being somewhat understated.  Chinese refined copper demand growth of over 9%, which is undeniably supporting global growth once again, takes account of slower growth in that country for the second half of this year (semis growth was up by 18% in H1), but should still be sufficient to outweigh any lingering concerns in the mature economies.  We still need to see better evidence of the end of re-stocking in these economies and a filter through to sustained end-use demand improvement before we make any significant upgrades to our H2 demand forecasts. 

**..while supply-side constraint provides further market support** Overall, the events of the past month have created a far more positive outlook

for the copper market moving forward (and certainly more optimistic than many macro indicators might suggest). Demand remains surprisingly strong in most developed economies supported by ongoing inventory adjustments and a general lack of scrap. Chinese consumption is clearly slowing but from unsustainably high levels and not at the sort of rates that were initially feared. In addition, mine supply disruptions remain as evident as ever (we have identified 400kt thus far in 2010 – see PRODUCTION) and refined output this year is thus likely to be little better than flat relative to 2009. Bringing all of this together leaves us with only a minimal surplus for this year and a sizeable deficit (-265kt) for 2011. Taking these changes into account we have lifted our average price forecast for 2010 to $6889/t ($3.12/lb) while for next year we are predicting an average of $7050/t ($3.20/lb). #### **Copper: LME cash prices & 3 month forward spread ($/t)** 10000 1000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2010 Page 5 of 21 Copper Monthly Update ## Consumption **Global primary copper demand forecast raised to 18.326Mt** We have made minor adjustments to our global primary copper demand forecast for this year, based largely on our understanding of second quarter market conditions in the USA and our expectations there for the second half. The 30kt increase in primary metal demand from last month is a reflection of higher demand estimated for Q2 (429kt now _vs._ last month’s 408kt) as well as increasing conviction that tightness in US scrap availability will force users to turn to more cathode in the second half. This particular comment about scrap availability, although perhaps not yet as strong, may well apply to large parts of northern Europe also going forward, and we are keeping an eye on these conditions over the summer months. We have not yet taken into account any such changes to the primary:secondary profile for Europe, but will do so this quarter if further user commentary supports such analysis. The change to the US demand increases our 2010 demand forecast on a global basis to 18.326Mt from last month’s 18.295Mt, leaving us with a year-on-year improvement of 6.3%. **Minor change to our Italian demand** The release this week of second quarter copper semis output in Italy has also prompted us to make minor changes to the quarter on quarter copper demand profile, if not to the overall 2010 forecast. Figures from Assomet, the Italian national metal semis association, point to much higher Q2 copper demand vs. Q1. Consequently, we have dropped slightly our Q1 estimate from 122kt to 118kt, and raised the same for Q2 from 154kt to 159kt.

### **USA** **US manufacturing activity continues to expand** US manufacturing activity remained in expansionary territory during June, as suggested by the latest purchasing manager’s index for the sector which reached 56.2 in June. However, the underlying strength behind the data has been declining in recent months, from 60.4 in April to May’s 59.7. With trade, retail sales and inventory data all showing reduced activity during June, it does appear that the US recovery is losing steam. Although industrial production growth of 8.2% in June would suggest otherwise, it is measured against June 2009 which was that year’s lowest point. More importantly, some leading indicators suggest that activity in July has weakened further, and that this will set the trend for Q3 and Q4 domestic copper demand. **Auto sector struggles in June…** Seasonally-adjusted auto production and sales figures for June were not very encouraging. While it would be tempting to accept the headline production increase of 9.8% on May and a 90% hike on June 2009 – which would suggest an annualised production of 8.62M units - the seasonally-adjusted 5% drop in output in June keeps an annualised forecast back at 7.55M units. Given that sales volumes have been flat for the past seven months, the generally poor conditions that exist for private auto purchases (low job security, reduced access to loans etc) are likely to keep the lid on any recovery in the sector. #### **US production of wire rod – (kt)** 30 125

**..as does construction…** Similarly, headline statistics behind the construction sector do not make for attractive reading. Mortgage applications have fallen in nine out of the past ten weeks to the slowest pace since 1996, and this will limit house sales in the coming months. House starts fell by 5% in June after a 15% drop in May to an annualised rate of 579k units, which is the lowest level in eight months; H1 starts to June are 5.8% down year-on-year. Although recent falls could be the reaction to the end of the home-builder tax credits which fell away in April, the hope was that there Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2010 Page 6 of 21 Copper Monthly Update would be a pick-up in construction activity by now. However, the fact that the home-builder survey fell to a 15-month low of just 14 in July suggests that the sector is some way off from improvement. Furthermore, the American Institute of Architects’ Billings Index fell by 2.5 points in May to 45.8 – its lowest rating in three months – and this reinforces the belief that the recovery anticipated for the construction sector for 2011 may be slower than previously thought. **..yet copper demand has been surprisingly strong*

* Despite the above general commentary on the two leading sectors in US copper markets, metal demand has held up fairly well.  Within the construction market, which accounts for c.50% of total US copper demand, clearly it has not been new starts that have been moving demand along but projects that are still being completed.  This has been seen more in building wire products than plumbing tube, which typically goes in later on in the project construction.  Meanwhile, magnet wire orders in both HVAC and automotive have been strong (although not back to the levels of 2007-2008), with lead times stretching out and backlogs stacking up.  Power cable is also reported to be strong because of considerable investment work being done across the country.  With the summer shut-downs having less of a detrimental impact on demand this year as they did a year ago when the economy generally was at its lowest point, order books still seem “reasonable” going forward, according to one major semis producers, but the concern is that there is a much reduced construction profile on the horizon.  Therefore, we interpret the market strength seen thus far as a reflection of the combined pressures of slowly improving demand at a time of historically low intermediate and finished product inventories.  Consequently, unless general economic conditions improve, we anticipate increasing inventories and softening product demand, with the latter forecast at 725kt for the second half, or 13% down on H1. 

**Wire rod mill orders turning down in July** One influential wire rod producer believes that US rod demand has been running at between 3-5% this year, with figures even double that for the months of June and July, although these were the worst two months of 2009.  A second rod producer believes the strong demand seen in May was due to re-stocking, but June’s orders reflected fresh underlying demand; meanwhile, his “reasonably healthy” order books for July could be due to the summer closure of at least two other principal rod plants, and he is somewhat concerned that, once they reopen, his business levels will suffer because there is little clarity much beyond August.  Apparent rod consumption for the first five months of this year, according to the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS), is closer to 2.2% over the same period last year.  Meanwhile, rod production data from the ABMS for the five months to May of 535.3kt (metric) was up 6.3% on the same period last year, and domestic shipments were up by 8.3%.  However, this year’s peak production level was in March (114.6kt), with May’s regressing to the Jan-Feb 2010 average of c.104kt. 

**Tube makers see relief from imports** As we reported in our May review, domestic tube makers are indeed seeing some benefit from the introduction of anti-dumping tariffs on copper tube imports from China and Mexico.  One maker claimed his company’s production line for residential ACR tube was now running flat out as opposed to the relative

ly low 65% back in January.  Although this comment would run counter to our observations of the residential construction build rates stated earlier, this new trade tariff has largely impacted this specific market and allowed his company to take full advantage of new orders from the air-conditioning OEMs.  With much of the USA already in the grip of a hot summer, AC manufacturers have been ramping up production rates anticipating a strong market through to the end of September.  By then, the joint investigation by the Commerce Department and International Trade Commission (ITC) into whether imports of Mexican and Chinese copper tube were being sold below market value in the US will have been completed, and whether or not the current tariff levies of 30% and between 10.26-60.5% on goods entering the US from those two countries, respectively, will remain in force. 

### **China** 

**Government “managing” economic slowdown** There have been mixed interpretations of the economic data emerging from China for June.  Because the data have generally shown month-on-month declines, it has been easy to take the view that, like in the US, the Chinese economy is running out of steam.  Industrial production growth, for example, “slowed” to 13.7% last month versus. June 2009 and down from May’s year-on-year growth of 16.5%.  Our view is that this “change” has been well engineered by the Chinese authorities who are steering for a soft economic landing for the next few months.  Real estate tightening measures will be maintained, for example, and these contributed to a near 1% contraction in property prices during June alone.  Even so, these measures have yet to have any significant impact on construction activity in the country, with floor space under construction increasing by almost 29% during the first half of this year over H1 2009, and investment in the sector increased by over 38%.  Equally, although auto production fell in June (by 1.8% on May) for the third straight month, we are still heading for a 25% year-on-year increase over 2009[can we give these numbers context – i.e. compared to the previous peak in 2007/8 or LT average?].  While auto sales have fallen at a faster rate than output (with the consequent build in stocks), the Chinese authorities will be considering introducing further tightening measures to reinforce their intent to cool the economy.  Restricting new loans will be the most likely way: by end-June, the government had already issued over 4.6Trn RMB in new loans, 62% of its full-year target. 

**Investment in power grid queried** Given the apparent need to slow down economic growth, there was a good deal of excitement but ultimately confusion among copper market analysts this month following the statement from the National Energy Administration that 200Bn RMB (US$29.5Bn) would be made available over the next 30 months _on top of_ what was already earmarked to upgrade the national grid and to take it to areas that have thus far gone with

out access to power.  While the sentiment to take power into hitherto neglected or under-resourced areas is valid, the financial sum and its relevance to copper consumption was misunderstood.  In terms of copper consumption, the _average_ spend

Page 7 of 21 

Copper Monthly Update 

invested in the grid over the past three years of 300Bn RMB last year has been due to the strong growth requirements of the infrastructure in urban areas due to high-profile events such as the Olympic Games and the Shanghai Expo.  But now the emphasis will go to rural grid upgrading programmes, and the total spend will be less than the 300Bn RMB of recent years, with rural programmes taking c.80Bn RMB of this amount.  For the first half of this year, the China Electricity Council reports that 121.4Bn RMB was spent on the grid, with a full year forecast being closer to 243Bn RMB, or 20% down on 2009’s 306Bn RMB.  No wonder, then, that most power cable manufacturers have been complaining recently that their order books are lighter this year than last.  Last year’s power grid investments “bought” c.2.7Mt of the red metal, according to some estimates, which accounted for roughly 40% of national copper demand.  But in a normal year, copper destined for power grid use accounts for only 30% of overall consumption. 

**Programme of subsidised sales of white goods remains strong…** China’s Ministry of Commerce reported that over 35.5M home appliance units were sold during the first half of this year under the subsidised sales programme, which was largely focused on rural areas in Henan, Shandong, Anhui, Hebei and Sichuan provinces.  June’s sales tally of 5.93M units far exceeded April’s 4.8M, with the top three products in terms of sales being refrigerators, television sets and water heaters.  The Ministry had previously announced that this old-for-new scheme will not only be extended to the end of 2011, but will expand its coverage from nine provinces and municipalities to 28. 

**..as does the “car exchange” programme** Despite the drop in overall auto sales last month, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology claims that it has lent 2.42Bn RMB during H1 to promote purchasing newer autos and get older models off the roads.  In May and June, almost 60,000 models were exchanged under the programme, with the monthly average for this year of 29k units being more than 9 times the level seen last year.  This programme runs alongside another which was rolled out at the end of June which is designed to promote the purchase of hybrid and other eco-friendly models.  While there are subsidies available of up to 50,000 RMB (US$7,400) for these models, in reality the programme extends this discount scheme to a much wider range of autos, albeit with lower rebates. 

**Semis production remains strong** Both the auto and home appliance rebate schemes should contribute to ongoing strength in national copper semis production ra

tes going forward. The China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNIA) reported total semis output was up for the first half of the year by almost 18% to 941.6kt on H1 2009, and continued investments in new plant will likely boost this further. This month Chinalco Kunming Copper Co began laying the foundations for a new 220kt/a semis plant, with stage one costing 1.47B RMB expected to initiate production 2011. There are some exceptions: for example, the Irish education department is clearly refurbishing schools during the summer holidays, and this has given rise to many sales opportunities for wire and cable products. But beyond such isolated circumstances, the sales boost seen a couple of months ago from re-stocking in the autos sector or healthy demand from the power sector has largely fallen away. Construction activity across Europe remains subdued and is unlikely to improve, given the widespread austerity measures that will span most countries in the region. Meanwhile, new power projects are staying on the drawing boards, and this will keep demand for power cable low for the quarter at least. Consequently, European copper demand is unlikely to manage even 2% growth this year. **Rod stock concern fades** With our general ex

pectation for a poorer regional demand for copper during H2 than in the first half, we expressed some dismay last month regarding rumours of a significant rod stock build by at least one major European wire rod producer.  However, we have since been able to clarify that such activity was planned ahead of plant shut-downs for maintenance.  The product stocks are likely to be brought down once the processing lines are returned to action by mid-August. 

**Usual buying patterns “no longer in force”** As we have learnt from other metals, we are finding that many European copper buyers throughout the process chain have one comment in common:  hand-to-mouth buying is here to stay.  Prior to the 2008 economic crash, the second quarter of any year, and the period between September-November were the strongest purchasing periods; Q1, August and then December were slack times.  Since 2008, most buyers have been ordering copper based on their perception of metal price trends: if prices are falling, they will wait until they believe prices are as low as they will go, and then will probably buy more than they will typically need versus booked orders purely because prices are deemed “favourable”.  This is especially so if – as is usual in the copper wire rod and sub-products businesses, where there are several small users – customers do not hedge material.  This implies a greater willingness to take on purchasing risk, and a probable increase in the use of the spot market.  It will also cloud any true assessment of the market as it will distort the traditional relationship between stock-builds and run-downs vis-а-vis first- and end-use demand. 

**Russia considers reinstatement of cathode export tax** Russia’s Finance Ministry repeated this month that it is considering reinstating the 10% export tax on refined copper cathode that it lifted back in February 2009.  With copper prices having risen considerably since then, the Ministry initially stated last September that it wanted to capture some of the value of national resources headed for overseas, but fell quiet on the matter until this month.  If it follows through, the export levy will come into force from January 2011.  However, producers of cathode will probably avoid the tax in the same way as they did the last time it was imposed by converting it into wire rod at domestic facilities, which is not being threatened with such an export tax.  Copper consumption averaged 680kt during the three-year period of 2006-2008 because cathode was processed into rod at home, but it plunged to just 330kt last year once that export duty was removed.  Our 2010 copper consumption forecast of 337kt reflects the absence of the cathode export tax, but our current forecast of 347kt for 2011 will move closer to 700kt if the 10% levy is reinstated from January 1<sup>st</sup> .  As yet, there is no word on the date that the Ministry will make its final decision, but in the interim it would not surprise us to see excess cathode be

ing drawn from stock for the export market if it is available, ahead of the levy. 

**Russian cathode exports continue to surge** As of May, Russian exports of cathode had already increased by 19% year-on-year to 210.3kt, with the Germany and Turkey being the most significant direct country customers and further amounts going into the Netherlands.  Whether the export levy comes into force or not next year, national cathode exports could increase now that UralElectromed’s Pyshma refinery has obtained LME certification, following an extensive quality improvement process that began as long ago as 2004.  While Pyshma has been selling good quality cathodes abroad, it has frequently had to sell at a discount to LME.  LME Good Delivery status now means that the company can command a Grade A premium which will help offset not just any export tax but also the usual freight costs.  It also means that Pyshma can use LME warehouses as a market of last resort for its production.

**Poor economic data brings into question Japan’s recovery** After almost one full year of uninterrupted economic growth, lower demand from export markets in May has put any ongoing recovery on hold. The PNG miner is reportedly meeting with its Korean and Japanese counterparts during the

**Rumours abound of smelters seeking “protection contracts”** One recurring rumour during the month was that certain smelters had been seeking some form of “protection contract” from miners.  In fact, this is not the first time that these rumours have surfaced because they first emerged during last year’s annual Mating Season.  While it is exceedingly difficult to verify whether such contracts have actually been entered into, there are a number of reasons why miners might be tempted into such deals.  With global primary smelter utilisation rates hovering just below 80% (against an optimal level of 88%) and with long-term and spot TC/RCs either at, or close to all-time lows, the chances of there being more casualties within the smelting sector appear ever more likely.  Also, as we have stated in the past, China’s growing dominance within the custom smelting market is very clearly evident.  Even more obvious is that country’s desire to continue expanding its smelting and refining base, regardless of whether such developments make sense commercially (at least in the short to medium term). 

**Chinese market dominance a concern in some quarters** It could be that China’s ongoing urge to raise its standing in the concentrates market may have more to do with a requirement to heighten its value added profile domestically. However, there remains the suspicion in some quarters that there could come a point where the Chinese industry becomes so dominant that it would be in a position to dictate not only concentrate market terms but perhaps the structure of custom smelting contracts.  This might take the form of TC/RCs no longer being quoted in dollars but in RMB, or indeed having metal prices referenced to the SHFE as opposed to the LME.  A further adjustment could be the raising of metallurgical deductions in deriving payable metals given that many Chinese smelters are unable to attain the high recoveries that are currently achieved by smelters within the developed economies.  Another potentially unwelcome contractual revision for miners could be the imposition or weighing and sampling at smelter gate as opposed to destination port (i.e. losses for the account of the miner between discharge port and inland smelters could be significant). 

**Should miners fear Chinese dominance in the custom smelting market?** Under the aforementioned circumstances a protection contract entered into between a miner and a smelter would not only ensure the long-term survivability of a preferred smelting customer but it could also serve to dilute the potential dominance of any emerging market force.  In order for such a contract to have any meaningful benefit to the smelter the TC/RCs would need to be fixed considerably above prevailing market rates and perhaps on a multi-year basis.  What is not clear about these contracts as a concept is how widespread their adoption would need to be in order to guarantee a stable market moving forward.  Also, as we h

ave highlighted in a previous review of this topic, the emergence of a dominant smelting force would be at the expense of many other existing smelters that would be forced to shut down.  Concentrate sellers could eventually reach a position whereby they either accept changes imposed by a dominant buyer or alternatively the deteriorating economics of custom smelting might reach a point at which acquiring a (cheap) shuttered tide water smelter/refinery to integrate with upstream mining operations becomes viable.

## Production news 

**Mine disruptions remain a feature of the copper market** Earlier this year we expressed concern as to whether copper mine disruptions moving forward would be as significant as they had been over the past five years.  Some of this concern arose from the fact that a number of prominent mines actually exceeded their 2009 production guidance last year, thereby partially offsetting disruptions elsewhere.  We questioned the need to apply a 6% generic initial disruption to our forecasts if, for example, the bottlenecks at manufacturers

of equipment, spare parts and consumables were perhaps easing on the premise that these suppliers would surely increase their capacity to overcome these issues.  We also wondered whether mining companies were applying more realistic, rather than optimistic production forecasts on the basis of prior experience.  However, our latest assessment of the disruptions to date in 2010 tells us that a significant disruption allowance remains justified in the forecasts.  Thus far this year we have identified over 300kt of losses from the concentrate producing sector and a further 100kt from SxEw producers against an initial expectation of 840kt for 2010 as a whole.  The major contributors to the disruptions to date include strikes at Vale’s Sudbury nickel/copper operations (now settled – see below) and at Voisey’s Bay, deferrals of high-grade ore extraction at Grasberg, a freeze on expenditure at First Quantum’s Frontier mine pending an ownership dispute, the slow reactivation of Cananea, earthquakes and lack of acid at some operations in Chile and the slow ramp up at Las Cruces in Spain.  Typically, up to 75% of all disruptions are due to a combination of technical issues, strikes and the slow ramp up of projects.  Assuming that high prices remain a feature of the market in the medium term then strikes will continue to be an issue, particularly in the Americas, although various companies have been successful in extending the life of labour contracts in order to prevent the frequency of industrial action.  Technical issues will remain a feature of the market although one might imagine that replacement lead times should be less than has been the case previously (for the reasons mentioned above).  The issue that we feel is most likely to dominate the disruption landscape over the next few years is the slow ramp up of projects, given the significant surge in capacity additions in the medium term.  To quantify this, over the period 2011 to 2013 gross additions to mine supply from greenfield and brownfield expansions are forecast to average 1.35Mt/a compared with an average of 0.75Mt/a over the period 2004 to 2009. 

**Strike ends at Vale Sudbury** Five days short of a full year spent on the picket lines, United Steelworkers Local 6500 and their brothers in Local 6200 at Vale’s Sudbury and Port Colborne operations, respectively, voted by 75% on 7-8<sup>th</sup> July to accept the latest offer tabled by Vale of a new five year contract.  Despite that relatively high apparent approval margin, it was a vote to return to work rather than one in favour of the new deal itself.  The main points of disagreement had centred on the terms of the nickel bonus (remuneration based on the portion of the nickel price above a predetermined threshold) and a defined benefits package for new employees.  Even with the new contracts now signed it is unlikely that all mines and facilities will return to work immediately and ramp up quickly with indications from Vale that this will ta

ke time.  The facilities will need much remediation after a year of closure and the company needs to assess not only how much of its workforce is still available (some positions have been vacated by retirement or by workers who have left the area to take up employment elsewhere).

**Konkola North to be developed** Vale and African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) are expected to invest $400M developing their Konkola North copper project in Zambia.  Vale aims to begin construction by September 2010 with production earmarked for 2013.  Initial output will be targeted at approximately 50kt/a copper-in-concentrates from 2.5Mt/a of ore, rising to 100kt/a in a phase II expansion by around 2015.  The decision for ARM to proceed with Konkola North is still subject to board approval which is scheduled to take place early in August.  Each company is expected to share the development cost equally. 

**Xstrata commits to Ernest Henry mine life extension** Following the Australian Government’s decision to exclude base metals mining from the proposed Mineral Resources Rent Tax (the new tax is intended to apply only to iron ore and coal resources from July 2012) Xstrata announced that it had reversed its earlier decision to suspend development activities at its Ernest Henry mine in Queensland.  Approved by the Xstrata board in December 2009, the A$589M Ernest Henry underground mine will extend the life of the operation by at least 12 years to 2024.  However, the project is still subject to final Queensland Government approvals.  The mine’s output was constrained to just 16.2kt Cu during H1 2010 due to the processing of low-grade stockpiled ores.  Milling activities are expected to switch back to higher-grade open pit ores during H2 which should raise copper output considerably (we estimate 65kt Cu for the year as a whole).  Low mine production at Ernest Henry coincided with a major re-bricking of the Mount Isa smelter, although refined production at Townsville was maintained at close to full capacity by treating more anodes that were shipped from the company’s Alt

onorte smelter in Chile. 

**First Quantum cuts back capital investment at Frontier pending ownership clarification** First Quantum Minerals (FQM) reported second quarter production of 85.4kt Cu which was lower than planned principally due to management’s decision to cut back capital investment at its 90kt/a Frontier mine during the quarter.  This decision was a consequence of the uncertainty regarding the future ownership of the Frontier mine following legal proceedings instigated by the DRC’s state-owned mining agency, Sodimico as regards to the latter’s request that its rights be reinstated on the “exclusive exploration zones” which Sodimico previously held and which were allegedly converted into a number of exploration licences now held by Frontier.  FQM will continue to manage the capital investment at Frontier in this manner until a satisfactory clarification of the decision by the Supreme Court is received.  As a result, the company’s total copper production estimate for 2010 has been revised downwards by 6.5% from 385kt to 360kt Cu. 

**Inmet continues to experience production problems at Las Cruces** Inmet Mining recently announced that a number of equipment failures and operational issues delayed the ramp-up of the Las Cruces plant and limited the ability to operate continuously.  As a result, cathode production was constrained to 6.6kt during the second quarter as compared to a target of 12.4kt, representing a utilisation rate of only 37% of the operation’s 72kt/a total capacity and 55% of available capacity.  The latter reflects the temporary constraint of having only two of the three leach residue filters available as one is currently dedicated to the neutralisation plant.  Installation of a new neutralisation filter means that the necessary additional filtration capacity should be available by the end of July. Production was also constrained in June by unexpected non-corrosion related equipment failures mostly related to the grinding and leach thickeners causing 10 days of lost production time. 

**Oz Minerals goes underground at Prominent Hill** Oz Minerals has approved the development of the underground extension to the Prominent Hill open pit mine in South Australia.  Preliminary work to access the Western Copper satellite deposit will begin immediately with first ore set to be extracted in Q4 2011.  The A$135M underground extension should contribute an incremental 25kt/a of copper-in-concentrates and 12koz/a of gold over a mine life of five years. During the first half of 2010 Prominent Hill produced 60.1kt of Cu and 90.8koz of Au.
